title: Final Accounts and Adjustments
lines: Final accounts questions on USAT ask you to find cost of goods sold, gross or net profit from a few figures, classify an item as capital or revenue, say where an item appears, or correct a draft profit for one or two adjustments. Keep a clear picture of which statement each item belongs to.
## The income statement
For a sole trader, the income statement has two parts. The trading account finds gross profit; the profit and loss account finds net profit.
- Net sales = Sales − Returns inwards
- Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Returns outwards + Carriage inwards − Closing stock
- Gross profit = Net sales − Cost of goods sold
- Net profit = Gross profit + Other incomes − Expenses
> Opening stock Rs 40,000, purchases Rs 260,000, carriage inwards Rs 6,000, returns outwards Rs 10,000, closing stock Rs 55,000.

Items in the profit and loss account include salaries, rent, carriage outwards, depreciation, bad debts and discount allowed (debits), and discount received, commission received and rent received (credits).
! Carriage inwards goes in the trading account as part of the cost of goods; carriage outwards is a selling expense in profit and loss. This pair is tested again and again.
## Mark-up and margin
Gross profit can be expressed on cost (mark-up) or on sales (margin). If goods are sold at cost plus 25 %, then sales are 125 % of cost and gross profit is 25/125 = 20 % of sales.
> Sales Rs 300,000 at cost plus 25 %. Cost = 300,000 × 100/125 = 240,000. Gross profit = Rs 60,000.
## The balance sheet

The balance sheet shows the position on one date. It lists non-current assets (land, buildings, machinery, vehicles, furniture, goodwill), current assets (stock, debtors, prepaid expenses, accrued income, bank, cash), capital, non-current liabilities (long-term loans) and current liabilities (creditors, outstanding expenses, income received in advance, bank overdraft).
- Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit − Drawings
- Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities
## Capital and revenue

Capital expenditure buys or improves a fixed asset that benefits more than one year: buying a van, extending a building, and the carriage, installation and legal costs needed to bring an asset into use. Revenue expenditure maintains the business from day to day: repairs, repainting, fuel, wages, rent. Capital receipts come from non-recurring sources (sale of a fixed asset, loans, new capital); revenue receipts come from normal trading (sales, commission, interest).
! Wages paid for installing a new machine are capital expenditure, added to the machine's cost. Ordinary wages are revenue. Treating capital expenditure as revenue understates both profit and assets.
## Adjustments

The trial balance shows what has been recorded. Adjustments bring each year's income and expense into line with the matching concept. Each adjustment has two effects: one in the income statement and one in the balance sheet.
| Adjustment | Income statement | Balance sheet
| Outstanding expense | Add to the expense | Current liability
| Prepaid expense | Deduct from the expense | Current asset
| Accrued income | Add to the income | Current asset
| Income received in advance | Deduct from the income | Current liability
| Depreciation | Expense in profit and loss | Deduct from the asset
| Further bad debts | Expense in profit and loss | Deduct from debtors
| Provision for doubtful debts | Charge the increase (or credit a decrease) | Deduct from debtors
| Closing stock | Credit of trading account | Current asset
| Goods taken by owner | Deduct from purchases | Add to drawings
> Insurance of Rs 36,000 is paid on 1 April for one year; the year ends on 31 December.
> April to December = 9 months: expense = 36,000 × 9/12 = Rs 27,000
> Prepaid (January to March) = Rs 9,000, a current asset
## Bad and doubtful debts
Bad debts are written off first; the provision for doubtful debts is then worked on the debtors that remain. Only the change in the provision affects this year's profit.
> Debtors Rs 200,000; write off Rs 5,000; provision 5 %.
> Remaining debtors 195,000; provision = 9,750
> Balance sheet: debtors 195,000 − 9,750 = Rs 185,250
! If the old provision was Rs 6,000 and the new one must be Rs 8,500, charge only Rs 2,500. A fall in the provision is a gain credited to profit and loss.
## Depreciation

Straight-line depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life, the same each year. Reducing balance applies a fixed percentage to the book value, so the charge falls each year. When an asset is bought during the year and the question says depreciation is for the time held, charge only the months owned.
## Correcting a draft profit
Work through each item and ask: does it raise or lower profit?
> Draft profit Rs 120,000; rent outstanding Rs 6,000; insurance prepaid Rs 2,000; depreciation of Rs 10,000 not charged.
An overstated closing stock raises this year's profit and, as next year's opening stock, lowers next year's profit by the same amount.
## Quick check
- Where do carriage inwards and carriage outwards go?
- How is income received in advance shown in the balance sheet?
- Why is only the increase in the provision charged?
- Is installation of a new machine capital or revenue expenditure?
